analysis.one_liner: Repeals ACA mandates, replaces subsidies with flat tax credits and HSAs, and turns Medicaid into block grants.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on this ACA replacement: it was referred to three committees and two subcommittees and expired with the 114th Congress, having drawn one Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican replacement for the Affordable Care Act repeals the requirements that individuals carry coverage and that large employers offer it, and ends federal rules requiring plans to cover a standard set of benefits and provide preventive care free. It swaps ACA income-based subsidies for a flat tax credit plus new health savings accounts, converts Medicaid's open-ended federal funding into fixed block grants, and lets states automatically enroll uninsured residents in high-deductible plans unless they opt out. It was sent to three House committees, then to subcommittees, and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers gain most directly: the mandate to offer affordable coverage and its reporting rules disappear, and they may reimburse workers' individual premiums without group-plan rules. Health insurers gain freedom from essential-benefit and free-preventive-care mandates and a new market for limited-benefit plans with annual dollar caps. Better-off uninsured adults gain a flat credit available at any income, unlike ACA subsidies that phase out at 400% of poverty. Banks and insurers gain a new Roth HSA product to administer, and concierge medicine practices are exempted from insurance regulation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large employers, insurers, healthier uninsured adults

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the employer mandate and its reporting rules, freeing large employers from penalties for not offering affordable coverage and letting them reimburse employees' individual premiums without group-plan rules.

Lifts ACA benefit mandates from insurers: no required essential health benefits, no required free preventive care, and permission to sell limited-benefit plans with annual dollar caps, which states must allow on their exchanges for residents to keep subsidies.

Creates a flat, advanceable, refundable tax credit of $2,500 per adult and $1,500 per child for people with qualifying coverage, available at any income, extending help above the ACA's 400%-of-poverty cutoff.

Lets states automatically enroll uninsured residents in a high-deductible default plan with a Roth HSA unless they opt out, and lets Medicaid enrollees choose a private plan with the credit surplus deposited into an HSA.

Protects the assets of patients whose capped-out limited-benefit plans leave them with medical bills, requires publication of cash prices for care paid from HSAs, and bars excessive charges for out-of-network emergency services.

analysis.who_pays: Medicaid enrollees bear the largest risk: federal payments become a fixed block grant, and states may not use the federal money for adults above 100% of the poverty line, so states absorb cost growth. People with serious illness or lapsed coverage face skinnier plans, returning annual benefit caps, and a 20% premium surcharge for each year without coverage. Anyone with large out-of-pocket medical costs loses the itemized deduction, and workers with generous employer plans face a clawback taxing the value of that benefit.

drawbacks.text: Reintroduces annual dollar caps on benefits: states must allow limited-benefit plans on their exchanges or residents lose subsidies, patients who hit the cap owe the remainder, providers may refuse further care outside emergencies, and only a bankruptcy-based share of the patient's property is protected from collection.
Imposes a 20% premium increase for each consecutive year an adult lacked coverage, a surcharge that falls hardest on people whose insurance lapsed for financial reasons.

Converts Medicaid's open-ended federal match into fixed payments and bars states from using the federal money for adults above 100% of the poverty line, leaving states to absorb cost growth and any coverage gaps.
Ends the requirements that plans cover a standard set of essential health benefits and provide preventive care at no cost, and eliminates the tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses.

The flat credit is limited to what a household actually pays in premiums and HSA deposits and is clawed back against the tax value of employer coverage, so people with premiums or employer plans worth more than the credit can end up worse off than under current law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a genuinely universal tax credit, default enrollment, and medical-debt protections with repeals that shift costs onto the people least able to bear them: block-granting Medicaid caps federal support as health costs grow, annual-limit plans and a 20%-a-year surcharge raise costs for people with gaps in coverage or serious illness, and required free preventive care disappears. Because it never advanced, the Congressional Budget Office never scored it, so even its supporters' claims about coverage and costs were never tested in the record.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to three committees and then to two subcommittees, but no committee ever approved it, no chamber ever voted, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions introduced the bill on May 19, 2016, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees.

On June 2, 2016 it went to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and on September 19, 2016 to the Education and the Workforce subcommittee on health, employment, labor, and pensions; neither committee reported it and no vote was ever scheduled.
Its only recorded support beyond the sponsor was one Republican cosponsor.
The bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, with no chamber ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the ACA's mandates, benefit standards, and open-ended Medicaid financing remained in place through the end of 2016, which is what employers, hospitals, and patients relying on those protections experienced, rather than the rewrite's sponsors.

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full replacement framework for the ACA on May 19, 2016.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 19, 2016; sent it to the Health Subcommittee on June 2, 2016; the committee never marked it up or reported it.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the bill's tax provisions (the credit, HSAs, mandate repeals) but never scheduled action.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral; sent it to the health subcommittee on September 19, 2016; the committee never reported it.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed unwinding the ACA; earlier in 2016 he had vetoed a Republican repeal package, signaling a veto of any similar bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all recorded support was Republican — the sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — and the Republican chairs of the three committees of referral never brought it up.

industries.note: The bill frees insurers from essential-benefit and free-preventive-care mandates and allows limited-benefit plans with annual dollar caps that qualify for subsidies, while keeping guaranteed issue, renewability, and risk adjustment. Their flexibility comes at the cost of thinner coverage for the people the subsidies are meant to protect.

The employer mandate, its penalties, and its reporting rules are repealed, and employers may reimburse workers' individual premiums without group-plan rules. Workers lose the federal guarantee that a large employer will offer affordable coverage, though generous employer plans face a new clawback tax unless the employer elects the Cadillac-tax regime.

The Medicaid block grant caps federal payment growth, and the asset-protection rules limit providers' ability to collect from patients whose capped-out plans leave bills — providers may also decline care beyond emergency obligations. Provider losses on funding and collections track losses in care access for poor patients.

The bill explicitly exempts concierge medicine from insurance regulation and lets HSA funds pay membership fees, legitimizing monthly-fee practices whose clients are mostly patients who can pay out of pocket.

industries.industry: Banks and insurers as HSA trustees
industries.note: Roth HSAs with a $5,000 annual limit create a new tax-advantaged product for banks and insurance companies to administer. The accounts mainly benefit households with money to save, so the gains skew up the income scale.
